cards.q: What makes the innate defenses nonspecific?
cards.a: They respond the same way to any invader, with no prior exposure required.
options: They grow faster and stronger with each repeat exposure to the same microbe
They are aimed at one antigen selected from a very large receptor library
They respond the same way to any invader, with no prior exposure needed
They act only against an invader the body has already met once before
cards.explanation: Innate defenses use a fixed set of recognition patterns shared by many microbes, so the response to a first encounter and a fiftieth encounter looks the same and starts within minutes. Requiring a prior encounter and growing stronger with repetition describe adaptive memory, which innate defenses do not have. Choosing one antigen from a large receptor library describes lymphocyte clonal selection, the defining feature of the specific arm.

cards.q: What does the lysozyme in tears and saliva do to bacteria?
cards.a: It digests the peptidoglycan of the bacterial cell wall.
options: It coats the bacterial surface so that phagocytes can grip it more easily
It builds a pore in the bacterial membrane out of complement proteins
It keeps the bacterium from attaching to the epithelial surface underneath
It breaks down the peptidoglycan that makes up the bacterial cell wall
cards.explanation: Lysozyme is an enzyme that cleaves the sugar backbone of peptidoglycan, so the wall fails and the bacterium bursts under its own osmotic pressure. Coating a surface for easier grip is opsonization, done by complement C3b and by antibody, not by lysozyme. Pore formation is the job of the membrane attack complex. Blocking attachment describes the physical role of mucus rather than an enzyme.

cards.q: Which leukocyte is most abundant in blood and arrives first in large numbers at an infected tissue?
cards.a: The neutrophil.
options: The monocyte
The eosinophil
The neutrophil
The basophil
cards.explanation: Neutrophils are roughly 60 to 70 percent of circulating white cells and are the first wave of phagocytes to leave the capillaries at an infection site. Monocytes arrive later and mature into macrophages that clean up debris. Eosinophils rise mainly with parasites and allergy, and basophils are rare cells that release histamine rather than doing bulk phagocytosis.

cards.q: What does a natural killer cell recognize on the cells it destroys?
cards.a: Body cells that have lost their normal self surface markers.
options: Free bacteria circulating in the blood and in the lymph
One specific antigen it was programmed in advance to match
Antibody coated proteins dissolved in the plasma
Body cells that have lost their normal self surface markers
cards.explanation: An NK cell surveys body cells for the self markers a healthy cell displays, and it kills the ones that have lost them, which is common in virus infected and tumor cells. Free bacteria are handled by phagocytes and complement, not by NK killing. Matching one preselected antigen describes a T or B lymphocyte, and NK cells act without that kind of specificity. Dissolved plasma proteins are not targets for a killing cell.

cards.q: What does interferon released by a virus infected cell do?
cards.a: It warns neighboring cells to make proteins that block replication.
options: It warns neighboring cells to make proteins that block replication
It binds the virus directly and keeps it from entering any host cell
It digests the protein coat of the virus once it is inside a cell
It draws neutrophils out of the blood and into the infected tissue
cards.explanation: Interferon is a warning signal, not a weapon. The infected cell is usually lost, but its interferon puts nearby cells into an antiviral state so the next round of virus meets resistance. Binding a virus directly to block entry is neutralization, which antibody does. Digesting a viral coat is not an interferon function, and drawing neutrophils into tissue is chemotaxis driven by chemokines and complement fragments.

cards.q: What does the membrane attack complex of complement do to a target cell?
cards.a: It forms a pore in the membrane so water and ions rush in and the cell lyses.
options: It forms a pore in the membrane so water and ions rush in and the cell lyses
It coats the target surface so that phagocytes bind and engulf it faster
It sets up a chemical gradient that draws phagocytes toward the infection
It forms a clot that seals the infected area off from the surrounding tissue
cards.explanation: The late complement proteins assemble into a ring that punches a hole in the membrane, and osmosis does the rest as water follows solute into the cell. Coating for easier engulfment and setting up a gradient are also real complement jobs, done by C3b (opsonization) and by smaller fragments (chemotaxis), which is exactly why they make good distractors here. Clotting walls off infection but is a function of fibrin, not complement.

cards.q: How does the mucociliary escalator of the airway protect the lungs?
cards.a: Cilia sweep particles trapped in mucus up toward the pharynx to be swallowed.
options: Cilia engulf and digest the particles that land on the airway surface
Cilia sweep particles trapped in mucus up toward the pharynx to be swallowed
Mucus triggers antibody release into the airway within a minute of exposure
Mucus kills inhaled bacteria with the strong acid that goblet cells secrete
cards.explanation: Mucus is the sticky trap and the cilia are the conveyor, moving the loaded mucus upward so the particles end up swallowed instead of settling in the alveoli. Airway mucus is not acidic; the strong acid barrier is in the stomach. Cilia are motile extensions and do not phagocytize. Antibody in secretions helps at mucosal surfaces, but it is an adaptive response that takes days, not a minute.

cards.q: Which chemical barrier destroys most swallowed bacteria before they reach the small intestine?
cards.a: Gastric acid, at a pH near 2.
options: Bile salts released into the duodenum
Gastric acid, which sits at a pH near 2
Mucus lining the wall of the esophagus
Surfactant secreted by the airway lining
cards.explanation: Stomach contents sit near pH 2, acidic enough to denature the proteins of most swallowed organisms before they ever reach the absorptive surface of the gut. Bile salts emulsify fat and enter downstream of the stomach. Esophageal mucus lubricates and shields the wall but does not kill. Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension and has nothing to do with the swallowed route.

cards.q: A child cannot make functional neutrophils. Which problem should you expect?
cards.a: Repeated bacterial infections with little pus at the infected site.
options: Failure to produce antibody after a routine childhood vaccination
Inability to raise body temperature at all during an infection
Loss of the skin barrier with widespread water loss through it
Repeated bacterial infections with little pus at the infected site
cards.explanation: Neutrophils do the bulk of early bacterial phagocytosis, and pus is largely spent neutrophils, so losing them means both frequent bacterial infection and an infected site that looks quiet rather than purulent. Antibody production is a B cell job and would be unaffected. Fever is set by the hypothalamus in response to pyrogens from macrophages and does not require neutrophils. The skin barrier is structural and independent of leukocyte counts.

cards.q: A large burn destroys the epidermis over a wide area. Which innate defense is lost first?
cards.a: The physical barrier that keeps microbes out.
options: The physical barrier that keeps microbes out of the tissue
The cellular defense provided by natural killer cells
The complement proteins circulating in the plasma
The chemical barrier provided by gastric acid
cards.explanation: Intact skin is the first line, a mechanical seal that microbes cannot cross, and a burn that removes the epidermis opens a wide door before any other defense is touched. Gastric acid guards the swallowed route and is unrelated to skin. NK cells and complement are still present and functional after a burn, which is why burn patients still mount responses once organisms get in; the problem is that organisms now get in easily.

cards.q: Complement fragments and bacterial products build up in an infected tissue. What do they do to neutrophils in nearby capillaries?
cards.a: They draw the neutrophils out toward the source of the signal.
options: They draw the neutrophils out toward the source of the signal
They make the neutrophils release antibody into the surrounding plasma
They keep the neutrophils from sticking to the wall of the vessel
They make the neutrophils divide rapidly while still inside the vessel
cards.explanation: This is chemotaxis: phagocytes follow the rising concentration of these molecules, and the same signals make them stick to the endothelium first so they can squeeze out. Neutrophils are end stage cells and do not divide in the bloodstream. Antibody secretion belongs to plasma cells. Preventing adhesion would block the response, the opposite of what these signals do.

cards.q: A bacterium becomes coated with the complement fragment C3b. What happens to the rate at which macrophages engulf it?
cards.a: It increases, because the coating gives the phagocyte a surface it can grip.
options: It stays the same, because phagocytes ignore anything coating a target
It increases, but only once antibody against the bacterium is also present
It increases, because the coating gives the phagocyte a surface it can grip
It decreases, because the coating hides the bacterial surface from view
cards.explanation: Macrophages carry receptors for C3b, so a coated bacterium is far easier to bind and pull in than a bare one. That process is opsonization, and it works whether or not antibody is around, which is why complement is useful on a first exposure. A coating that hid the surface would be a bacterial defense, like a capsule, not a host one.

cards.q: A patient is given interferon during a viral illness. Which cells does it act on to slow the infection?
cards.a: The uninfected cells nearby, which it readies against the virus.
options: The B cells, which it drives to secrete antibody more quickly
The uninfected cells nearby, which it readies against the virus
The already infected cells, which it destroys outright
The virus particles in plasma, which it binds and neutralizes
cards.explanation: Interferon protects the cells that have not yet been infected by inducing enzymes that shut down viral protein synthesis if the virus arrives. It does not kill the cell that released it, and it does not bind virus particles, which is antibody work. Driving antibody secretion is a cytokine effect of helper T cells, not the antiviral action interferon is named for.

cards.q: A person is infected with the same bacterium a second time. How does the innate response compare with the first time?
cards.a: It is the same speed and the same size, because innate defenses store no memory.
options: It is absent, because the adaptive system now handles this organism alone
It is faster and larger, because innate cells remember the first exposure
It is the same speed and the same size, because innate defenses store no memory
It is slower, because the first exposure used up the available innate cells
cards.explanation: Innate recognition is genetically fixed, so a repeat exposure gets an identical response beginning within minutes. Faster and larger on repeat exposure describes the adaptive secondary response, which is happening at the same time but is a different system. Innate cells are continually replaced from bone marrow, so they are not used up, and innate defenses do not switch off once adaptive immunity exists.

cards.q: A splinter drives bacteria into the dermis. Which cell meets them first, before any new cells arrive from the blood?
cards.a: The macrophage already resident in the tissue.
options: The helper T cell waiting in the nearest lymph node
The macrophage already resident in the tissue
The neutrophil arriving from the bloodstream
The plasma cell secreting antibody into the wound
cards.explanation: Tissues are patrolled by resident macrophages that are on site at time zero, which is why they are the cells that detect the invasion and release the signals that call everyone else. Neutrophils are fast but still have to marginate and cross the vessel wall, which takes an hour or more. Plasma cells and helper T cells belong to the adaptive response and act days later.

cards.q: A patient's neutrophils reach an infected tissue in normal numbers and engulf bacteria normally, but the bacteria survive inside them. Which step failed and what follows?
cards.a: Killing inside the phagosome failed, so the engulfed bacteria survive and the infection persists.
options: Adherence failed, so the phagocytes cannot bind the bacteria at all
Killing inside the phagosome failed, so the engulfed bacteria survive
Diapedesis failed, so the phagocytes cannot leave the capillary at all
Chemotaxis failed, so bacteria spread while phagocytes stay in the blood
cards.explanation: Phagocytosis has ordered steps: chemotaxis, adherence, engulfment, then digestion in the phagolysosome. The case states that the cells arrived and engulfed normally, so the first three steps worked and only the killing step is left. Chemotaxis and diapedesis failures would show up as phagocytes that never reach the tissue, and an adherence failure would prevent engulfment, which the case explicitly says occurred.

cards.q: A virus stops its host cell from displaying the self markers that cytotoxic T cells read. Predict the effect on natural killer cell activity against that cell.
cards.a: NK killing increases, because missing self markers is what NK cells act on.
options: NK killing increases, because missing self markers is what NK cells act on
NK killing decreases, because NK cells need those markers to find a target
NK killing is unchanged, because NK cells respond only to antibody coating
NK killing stops, because NK cells act only when a helper T cell approves
cards.explanation: The two systems are complementary: a cytotoxic T cell needs the display, and an NK cell kills when the display is missing, so a virus that hides the markers escapes one system and walks into the other. NK cells do not need the markers to identify a target, they need their absence. They also do not require antibody or helper T permission, which is what lets them act on the first day of an infection.

cards.q: A patient makes normal antibody and has normal phagocytes but lacks the late complement proteins. Which defense is lost while the rest stays intact?
cards.a: Direct lysis is lost, though opsonization and chemotaxis are intact.
options: Antibody production is lost, since complement is what activates B cells
Opsonization is lost, so phagocytes can no longer bind bacteria at all
Direct lysis is lost, though opsonization and chemotaxis are intact
Chemotaxis is lost, so phagocytes no longer migrate toward an infection
cards.explanation: The complement cascade splits into early components, which produce C3b for opsonization and small fragments for chemotaxis, and late components, which build the membrane attack complex. Losing only the late proteins removes lysis and leaves the early functions working. Opsonization and chemotaxis would be lost with an early block instead. Complement supports antibody responses but does not create them, so B cells still work.

cards.q: After a week of broad spectrum antibiotics a patient develops diarrhea from a resistant organism that has overgrown the colon. Which innate defense was weakened, and why does overgrowth follow?
cards.a: Competition from the resident flora was lost, and without it an invader has open space and nutrients.
options: Natural killer surveillance of the intestinal lining was suppressed by the drug
Gastric acid was neutralized, so swallowed organisms now survive the stomach
Complement lysis failed, since complement requires intact gut flora to work
Competition from the resident flora was lost, leaving space and nutrients open
cards.explanation: The normal flora is a nonspecific defense: it occupies attachment sites and consumes nutrients, so a newcomer has nowhere to establish. An antibiotic that clears the flora removes that competition, and a resistant organism expands into the empty niche. Antibiotics do not change gastric pH, complement works independently of gut bacteria, and NK cells are not the defense being removed here.

cards.q: What are the four classic cardinal signs of acute inflammation?
cards.a: Redness, heat, swelling, and pain.
options: Bruising, heat, dryness, and weakness
Redness, heat, swelling, and pain
Pallor, coolness, swelling, and numbness
Redness, coolness, shrinkage, and itching
cards.explanation: Each sign traces to a vascular change: redness and heat from arteriolar dilation, swelling from increased capillary permeability, and pain from mediators plus pressure on nerve endings. Pallor and coolness would mean reduced blood flow, the opposite of what inflammation does. Shrinkage and dryness are not features of an inflamed tissue, which gains fluid rather than losing it.

cards.q: Which cell releases the histamine that starts the vascular changes of inflammation?
cards.a: The mast cell.
options: The mast cell
The plasma cell
The helper T cell
The natural killer cell
cards.explanation: Mast cells sit in connective tissue right where injury occurs and degranulate within seconds, dumping preformed histamine into the interstitium. Plasma cells secrete antibody days later, helper T cells release cytokines that direct adaptive responses, and NK cells kill abnormal body cells. None of the three carries the histamine granules that start the vascular response.

cards.q: What does histamine do to the arterioles supplying an injured area?
cards.a: It dilates them, increasing local blood flow.
options: It stiffens their walls without changing their diameter
It dilates them only after the tissue has finished healing
It constricts them, reducing local blood flow
It dilates them, increasing local blood flow
cards.explanation: Arteriolar dilation is the first vascular event, and it is what delivers the extra blood that makes the area red and warm. Constriction would reduce delivery of plasma proteins and phagocytes, the opposite of what the response needs. Vessel walls do not stiffen during inflammation, and the dilation happens within minutes of injury, not after repair.

cards.q: Which change in the capillaries produces the swelling of inflammation?
cards.a: Increased permeability, which lets fluid and protein leave the blood.
options: Increased velocity of blood through the capillary bed
Decreased hydrostatic pressure inside the capillary itself
Increased permeability, which lets fluid and protein leave the blood
Decreased permeability, which traps fluid inside the capillary lumen
cards.explanation: Mediators such as histamine make endothelial cells pull apart, and fluid with plasma protein moves into the interstitium, which is the edema you can see and feel. Decreased permeability would keep fluid in the vessel and produce no swelling. Faster flow does not by itself push fluid out, and a fall in capillary hydrostatic pressure would favor reabsorption, again the wrong direction.

cards.q: What is diapedesis?
cards.a: Leukocytes squeezing between endothelial cells to leave the vessel.
options: Leukocytes squeezing between endothelial cells to leave the vessel
Leukocytes sticking to the vessel wall just before they exit it
Leukocytes migrating along a chemical gradient within the tissue
Leukocytes engulfing and digesting a bacterium they have bound
cards.explanation: Diapedesis is the crossing step, when a leukocyte deforms and slips through the gap between endothelial cells into the tissue. Sticking to the wall beforehand is margination, following the gradient once outside is chemotaxis, and engulfing the organism is phagocytosis. These are four consecutive steps, and separating them in order is exactly what this competency asks for.

cards.q: What do pyrogens do at the hypothalamus?
cards.a: They raise the temperature set point the hypothalamus defends.
options: They keep the hypothalamus from sensing the temperature of the blood
They increase heat loss by dilating the blood vessels of the skin
They raise the temperature set point the hypothalamus defends
They lower the set point so that the body begins to cool itself
cards.explanation: A pyrogen resets the thermostat upward, and the body then uses its ordinary heat gaining reflexes to reach the new target. Lowering the set point and increasing skin heat loss are what an antipyretic causes once the pyrogen is blocked. The hypothalamus continues to sense blood temperature perfectly well during fever, which is why it can defend the higher value so precisely.

cards.q: Which cell arrives at an inflamed site after the neutrophils and clears debris and dead cells?
cards.a: The monocyte, which becomes a macrophage in the tissue.
options: The natural killer cell, which lyses cells with abnormal markers
The monocyte, which becomes a macrophage once in the tissue
The neutrophil, which arrives in the first hours after injury
The plasma cell, which secretes antibody into the tissue fluid
cards.explanation: Monocytes follow the neutrophil wave by roughly a day, transform into macrophages, and do the long duty of ingesting debris, dead neutrophils, and remaining organisms while releasing signals for repair. The neutrophil is the early responder named in the stem itself. Plasma cells and NK cells have real jobs in defense but neither is the debris clearing cell of an inflamed wound.

cards.q: What is pus made of?
cards.a: Dead neutrophils, tissue debris, and fluid.
options: Clotted blood and fibrin strands only
Antibody rich plasma containing no cells
Lymph draining out of the injured region
Dead neutrophils, tissue debris, and fluid
cards.explanation: Neutrophils die where they work, and the accumulation of spent cells with liquefied debris is what you see as pus, which is why a patient who cannot make neutrophils forms very little of it. A clot is fibrin and trapped red cells and looks quite different. Cell free plasma and lymph are clear fluids, not the thick creamy material that defines an abscess.

cards.q: Why does an inflamed area look red and feel warm?
cards.a: Arteriolar dilation increases blood flow, bringing more warm blood to the area.
options: Arteriolar dilation increases blood flow, bringing more warm blood to it
Fluid leaking into the tissue space raises the local temperature directly
Neutrophils generate heat as a byproduct of digesting the bacteria
Blood flow slows down, so blood lingers long enough to warm the tissue
cards.explanation: Redness and heat are one mechanism seen two ways: more blood in the area means more hemoglobin visible through the skin and more core temperature blood delivered to a surface that is normally cooler. Edema fluid arrives at the same temperature as the blood it came from and adds no heat of its own. Phagocytosis does not generate measurable local warming, and slowed flow would make an area look dusky and feel cool.

cards.q: Aspirin reduces inflammatory pain by blocking prostaglandin synthesis. What does that tell you about prostaglandins at an injury?
cards.a: They sensitize pain endings so that ordinary stimuli begin to hurt.
options: They pull fluid out of the tissue and return it to the capillary blood
They sensitize pain endings so that ordinary stimuli begin to hurt
They constrict local vessels and reduce blood flow to the injured tissue
They kill bacteria directly in the fluid surrounding the injured cells
cards.explanation: If removing prostaglandins removes pain, prostaglandins must be part of what generates it, and their role is to lower the threshold of nociceptors so that light pressure on a sore finger is felt as pain. Prostaglandins in inflammation promote dilation rather than constriction. They have no antibacterial activity, and they favor fluid leaving the capillary rather than returning to it.

cards.q: A splinter enters the dermis. Which sequence of events follows?
cards.a: Chemical release, then vasodilation, then increased permeability, then leukocyte exit.
options: Vasodilation, chemical release, leukocyte exit, increased permeability
Leukocyte exit, chemical release, vasodilation, increased permeability
Increased permeability, leukocyte exit, vasodilation, chemical release
Chemical release, vasodilation, increased permeability, leukocyte exit
cards.explanation: Damaged cells and resident mast cells release mediators first, and everything downstream is a response to those signals: vessels dilate, then they leak, then leukocytes stick and cross the wall. Any order that puts a vascular change before the chemical signal reverses cause and effect. Leukocyte exit has to come last of the four, because the cells need the adhesion signals and the widened gaps in order to leave.

cards.q: Why does inflammatory edema fluid contain far more protein than the fluid normally filtered from a capillary?
cards.a: The widened gaps between endothelial cells let plasma protein pass through.
options: Capillary hydrostatic pressure falls sharply during an inflammatory response
Lymphatic vessels actively pump protein from the blood into the tissue
Neutrophils manufacture and secrete protein into the interstitial fluid
The widened gaps between endothelial cells let plasma protein pass through
cards.explanation: A normal capillary holds protein back, so ordinary filtrate is nearly protein free; inflammation changes the wall itself, and once the gaps are wide enough albumin follows the water out. Hydrostatic pressure actually rises in inflammation because of upstream dilation. Lymphatics drain protein away from tissue rather than delivering it, and the protein in an exudate comes from plasma, not from neutrophil synthesis.

cards.q: A patient's hypothalamic set point has just risen to 39 C while body temperature is still 37 C. What does the patient feel and do?
cards.a: Feels cold and shivers, because the body is now below its set point.
options: Feels hot and dilates skin vessels, because heat production has risen
Feels cold and shivers, because the body is now below its set point
Feels hot and sweats, because the set point has risen above normal
Feels normal, because 37 C is a perfectly normal body temperature
cards.explanation: The hypothalamus compares actual temperature with the set point, and a 2 degree gap in that direction is read as being too cold no matter what the absolute number is. Shivering and skin vasoconstriction follow, which is why the chills of a rising fever feel so convincing. Sweating and skin vasodilation are heat loss responses and occur when actual temperature is above the set point, which happens later when the fever breaks.

cards.q: Aspirin brings a fever down. What has it done to the hypothalamic set point?
cards.a: It lowered the set point, so heat loss responses turn on.
options: It blocked the skin receptors from sensing temperature at any level
It cooled the blood directly as the blood passed through the skin
It lowered the set point, so heat loss responses such as sweating turn on
It raised the set point further, so the patient begins shivering again
cards.explanation: Antipyretics work upstream, by blocking the prostaglandin that raised the set point, so the thermostat returns toward 37 C and the body, now above target, sweats and dilates skin vessels until temperature falls. Raising the set point is what the pyrogen did. The drug does not act on skin receptors and does not cool blood directly; the cooling is the body's own response to a corrected set point.

cards.q: How does a moderate fever aid defense?
cards.a: It speeds immune cell activity and slows the growth of many pathogens.
options: It speeds immune cell activity and slows the growth of many pathogens
It denatures every bacterial protein once temperature passes 39 C
It removes the need for phagocytes to enter the infected tissue
It stops histamine release and so brings the swelling to an end
cards.explanation: A few degrees raises the rate of nearly every enzymatic and cellular process, including phagocyte movement and lymphocyte proliferation, while many pathogens replicate best at 37 C and do less well above it. Bacterial proteins are not denatured at 39 C; temperatures that would do that would kill the patient first. Fever supports phagocytes rather than replacing them, and it does not end the swelling.

cards.q: A person takes an antihistamine immediately after an insect sting. Predict the effect on local blood flow and on swelling.
cards.a: Blood flow falls and swelling is reduced, since both follow histamine.
options: Blood flow rises but swelling is reduced, since the two changes are unrelated
Blood flow falls while swelling increases, since fluid can no longer drain away
Blood flow and swelling are both unchanged, since histamine only causes itching
Blood flow falls and swelling is reduced, since both follow histamine action
cards.explanation: Histamine does two things at once, dilating arterioles and opening gaps between endothelial cells, so blocking its receptors reduces both the extra flow and the leak that follows it. The two effects cannot separate, since they come from the same mediator acting on the same vascular bed. Antihistamines do not impair lymphatic drainage, and histamine drives far more than itching, which is why the drug works on the swelling too.

cards.q: A patient on a drug that strongly suppresses inflammation cuts a finger. Predict what happens to the redness and to bacterial clearance.
cards.a: Less redness and slower bacterial clearance, since phagocyte delivery falls with the vascular response.
options: No change in either, since inflammation does not affect phagocyte delivery
Less redness and slower clearance, since phagocyte delivery also falls
Less redness and faster clearance, since fewer cells crowd the site of injury
More redness and slower clearance, since the vessels remain dilated throughout
cards.explanation: The cardinal signs are not side effects of defense, they are the delivery system: dilation and leakage bring the phagocytes and plasma proteins to the wound. Suppress the vascular response and you lose both the visible signs and the delivery, so infection clears more slowly. That trade is the reason anti inflammatory therapy raises infection risk, and it is why the option pairing less redness with faster clearance is the one students most often want to choose.

cards.q: An inflamed ankle is swollen although the patient has normal plasma albumin, normal venous pressure, and normal lymphatic drainage. Working back from the swelling, what explains it?
cards.a: Increased capillary permeability caused by inflammatory mediators.
options: Increased capillary permeability caused by inflammatory mediators
Reduced plasma colloid osmotic pressure from a low albumin level
Raised venous pressure backing fluid up in the capillary bed
Blocked lymphatic drainage from the whole of the affected limb
cards.explanation: Edema has four classic causes, and this case rules out three of them by stating that albumin, venous pressure, and lymph drainage are all normal, which leaves a change in the capillary wall itself. Inflammatory mediators do exactly that, opening gaps so both fluid and protein escape. Each of the other three would produce swelling under different conditions, which is why they are worth knowing, but none of them fits the findings here.

cards.q: A febrile child suddenly begins sweating heavily and her skin flushes. What changed at the hypothalamus, and what happens to core temperature next?
cards.a: The set point fell, so heat loss responses bring core temperature down.
options: The hypothalamus stopped regulating, so temperature will now drift freely
The set point is unchanged, so the sweating will not alter temperature
The set point fell, so heat loss responses bring core temperature down
The set point rose, so heat production will push temperature higher still
cards.explanation: When the pyrogen clears, the thermostat drops back toward 37 C while the body is still at 39 C, so the patient is suddenly above target and turns on sweating and skin vasodilation. Those responses are the fever breaking, and temperature falls over the next hour. A rising set point produces the opposite picture, shivering and pale cool skin, and a hypothalamus that had stopped regulating would not produce a coordinated heat loss response at all.

cards.q: Which cell is responsible for humoral immunity?
cards.a: The B lymphocyte.
options: The cytotoxic T lymphocyte
The tissue macrophage
The natural killer cell
The B lymphocyte
cards.explanation: Humoral immunity is named for the body fluids, and its agent is the B cell, whose descendants pour antibody into blood and lymph. The cytotoxic T cell carries out cell mediated immunity instead, killing infected cells directly. Macrophages and NK cells contribute to defense but belong to the innate side and do not produce antibody.

cards.q: An activated B cell divides. What do most of its daughter cells become, and what do they secrete?
cards.a: Plasma cells, which secrete antibody.
options: Plasma cells, which secrete antibody
Cytotoxic cells, which secrete perforin
Memory T cells, which secrete cytokines
Macrophages, which secrete digestive enzymes
cards.explanation: The effector form of a B cell is the plasma cell, packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum and dedicated to antibody export; a smaller share of the daughters become memory B cells instead. Perforin comes from cytotoxic T cells and NK cells. A B cell cannot become a T cell or a macrophage, since those arise from separate lineages.

cards.q: Which targets does humoral immunity handle best?
cards.a: Bacteria and toxins that are free in the blood and lymph.
options: Cells of a transplanted organ from another person
Bacteria and toxins free in the blood and in the lymph
Viruses that are already replicating inside a body cell
Tumor cells growing in the middle of a solid tissue
cards.explanation: Antibody is a soluble protein that circulates in body fluids, so it can only reach a target that is also out in those fluids: extracellular bacteria, free virus particles between cells, and dissolved toxins. Anything hidden inside a cell, including a replicating virus, a tumor cell, or a graft cell, has to be handled by cell mediated immunity, because antibody cannot cross the plasma membrane to reach it.

cards.q: Which cell directly kills a virus infected body cell?
cards.a: The cytotoxic T cell.
options: The cytotoxic T cell
The plasma cell
The helper T cell
The B cell
cards.explanation: The cytotoxic T cell is the killer of the adaptive system: it inspects a cell's surface display and destroys the cell if the display includes foreign fragments. Plasma cells and B cells work through secreted antibody and never touch a target cell. Helper T cells direct the response with cytokines but do not deliver the lethal hit themselves.

cards.q: How does a cytotoxic T cell kill its target?
cards.a: It releases perforin and granzymes that trigger apoptosis in the target.
options: It secretes antibody that coats the target cell and dissolves it
It cuts off the target cell's supply of oxygen and glucose
It releases perforin and granzymes that trigger apoptosis in the target
It engulfs the target cell whole and digests it in a lysosome
cards.explanation: Perforin opens a channel in the target membrane and granzymes enter through it to trigger the cell's own suicide program, which kills the cell and its viral contents together with little spill into the tissue. Engulfing a whole cell is what a macrophage does. T cells never secrete antibody, and no immune cell kills by starving a target of oxygen or glucose.

cards.q: What is the main job of the helper T cell?
cards.a: It releases cytokines that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
options: It engulfs bacteria in tissue and digests them in a phagosome
It releases cytokines that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells
It lyses infected body cells directly using perforin and granzymes
It secretes the bulk of the antibody produced during a response
cards.explanation: The helper T cell is the hub of the adaptive response: it reads displayed antigen and then licenses both arms with chemical signals, which is why losing it damages antibody and killing responses at the same time. Direct lysis is the cytotoxic T cell's role, antibody secretion belongs to plasma cells, and phagocytosis is done by macrophages and neutrophils.

cards.q: Which cell engulfs an antigen and displays a fragment of it to a helper T cell?
cards.a: The dendritic cell.
options: The plasma cell
The cytotoxic T cell
The red blood cell
The dendritic cell
cards.explanation: Dendritic cells and macrophages are the professional antigen presenting cells: they take material in from the tissue, break it down, and hold a fragment on the surface where a helper T cell can read it. A plasma cell is a secretory end cell and presents nothing. Cytotoxic T cells read displays rather than create them, and red cells have no nucleus and no presenting machinery.

cards.q: What does clonal selection mean?
cards.a: An antigen binds the lymphocyte whose receptor already fits it and drives that cell to divide.
options: Every lymphocyte in the body responds to every antigen that enters the body
The thymus builds a brand new receptor design after each separate infection
An antigen binds the lymphocyte whose receptor already fits and expands it
A lymphocyte reshapes its receptor until it fits the antigen it has just met
cards.explanation: The receptor repertoire is generated before any antigen is seen, so an infection does not teach the immune system anything new; it selects the rare cell that already matched and expands it into a clone. That is why the response takes days on a first exposure, since the starting population is tiny. Receptors do not reshape themselves to fit, and a response involving every lymphocyte would have no specificity at all.

cards.q: A bacterial toxin circulating in the plasma is bound and inactivated before it can reach its target tissue. Which arm of adaptive immunity did that?
cards.a: Humoral immunity, using antibody against an extracellular target.
options: Humoral immunity, using antibody against an extracellular target
Cell mediated immunity, using cytotoxic T cells against the toxin
Cell mediated immunity, using helper T cells to digest the toxin
Innate immunity, using natural killer cells to lyse the toxin
cards.explanation: A dissolved toxin is extracellular, so the tool that reaches it is a soluble one, and antibody binding that blocks the toxin from attaching to its target is neutralization. Cytotoxic T cells kill cells and cannot act on a free molecule. Helper T cells signal and do not digest anything, and NK cells lyse abnormal body cells, not molecules.

cards.q: A body cell infected with a virus is destroyed while neighboring healthy cells are left alone. Which arm did this, and how did it choose the target?
cards.a: Cell mediated immunity, by reading foreign fragments displayed on the infected cell surface.
options: Humoral immunity, with antibody dissolving the membrane of the infected cell
Cell mediated immunity, killing any cell found near the site of the infection
Cell mediated immunity, reading foreign fragments displayed on the cell surface
Humoral immunity, with antibody entering the cell and killing the virus inside
cards.explanation: A cell that is making viral protein puts pieces of it on its surface, and a cytotoxic T cell whose receptor matches that fragment kills only the cells carrying it, which is what spares the neighbors. Antibody cannot cross into a cell, and antibody does not dissolve membranes on its own. Killing everything nearby would describe indiscriminate damage rather than the targeted mechanism this arm uses.

cards.q: A transplanted kidney is attacked and destroyed by the recipient's immune system. Which arm carries the main burden of that rejection?
cards.a: Cell mediated immunity, because the targets are whole cells from another person.
options: Humoral immunity, because antibody is the only defense against foreign tissue
Innate immunity, because rejection begins within seconds of the transplant
Neither arm, because transplanted tissue is not recognized as foreign at all
Cell mediated immunity, because the targets are whole cells from another person
cards.explanation: Graft cells display surface markers the recipient's T cells read as foreign, so the destruction follows the same route as killing an infected cell: T cell recognition then direct attack. Antibody can contribute to rejection but is not the main mechanism and cannot handle intact cells the way T cells do. Rejection develops over days to weeks, not seconds, and foreign tissue is very much recognized, which is the whole problem.

cards.q: A virus destroys a patient's helper T cells. Predict the effect on antibody production.
cards.a: It falls, because B cells depend on helper T signals to mount a full response.
options: It stops within a day, because helper T cells make all the antibody
It falls, because B cells depend on helper T signals for a full response
It rises, because B cells are released from helper T cell inhibition
It is unchanged, because B cells work entirely on their own
cards.explanation: Most antigens require B cells to receive cytokine help from an activated helper T cell before they proliferate and switch to high output antibody secretion, so losing helpers weakens the humoral arm even though the B cells themselves are intact. Helper T cells stimulate rather than inhibit, so removing them cannot raise output. They also secrete no antibody themselves, and the decline develops over months rather than in a day.

cards.q: Why does antibody alone fail to clear a virus that is already inside a host cell?
cards.a: Antibody cannot enter a cell, so the infected cell itself has to be killed.
options: Antibody cannot enter a cell, so the infected cell itself has to be killed
Antibody is broken down by stomach acid before it can reach the cell
Antibody binds only sugars, and viral particles are built only of protein
Antibody works only after the infected cell has already died on its own
cards.explanation: Antibody is a large plasma protein and stays outside cells, so it is excellent at catching virus in transit between cells and useless against a virus replicating within one. Clearing that infection needs a cytotoxic T cell to destroy the factory. Stomach acid is irrelevant to antibody in the tissues, antibody binds protein epitopes readily, and waiting for the cell to die would let the virus finish replicating first.

cards.q: A body cell is displaying a fragment of a protein it made itself from viral instructions. Which cell reads that display?
cards.a: The cytotoxic T cell, which inspects what a cell is making inside.
options: The helper T cell, which inspects only material engulfed from outside
The B cell, which binds only antigen that is free in the tissue fluid
The plasma cell, which reads displays before it secretes its antibody
The cytotoxic T cell, which inspects what a cell is making inside itself
cards.explanation: Displays of a cell's own internal products are read by cytotoxic T cells, which is how any nucleated cell reports what it is manufacturing and how an infected one gives itself away. Helper T cells read the other display route, the one that carries material an antigen presenting cell took in from outside, so mixing these two up is the classic error here. B cells bind free antigen directly, and plasma cells simply secrete.

cards.q: A bacterium survives inside macrophages rather than in the tissue fluid. Which arm is needed to control it?
cards.a: Cell mediated immunity, because the target is inside a cell.
options: Humoral immunity, because the target is a bacterium rather than a virus
Neither arm, because a macrophage is part of the innate defenses
Cell mediated immunity, because the target now sits inside a cell
Humoral immunity, because antibody can follow the bacterium into the cell
cards.explanation: The arm you need is set by where the target is, not by what kind of organism it is, so a bacterium hiding inside a cell is a cell mediated problem just as a virus would be. Antibody cannot follow it in. Classifying by organism type is the trap in this card, and thinking that innate cells are off limits to adaptive help misses the fact that T cells activate macrophages to kill what they hold.

cards.q: An infant is born without a thymus but makes B cells normally. Predict what happens to cell mediated immunity and to antibody responses that require helper T cells.
cards.a: Cell mediated immunity fails and helper dependent antibody responses are weak.
options: Cell mediated immunity fails but every antibody response remains fully normal
Cell mediated immunity is normal while antibody responses fail completely
Both arms stay normal, because B cells can take over the work of T cells
Cell mediated immunity fails and helper dependent antibody responses are weak
cards.explanation: T cells mature in the thymus, so no thymus means no functional T cells of either kind. That wipes out cell mediated immunity outright and also cripples the humoral responses that need helper T cytokines, even though the B cells themselves are present and healthy. Expecting antibody to be untouched is the common mistake, because it treats the two arms as independent when helper T cells sit upstream of both.

cards.q: Trace the humoral response to a bacterium that enters through a cut. Which order of events is correct?
cards.a: Antigen presentation, helper T activation, B cell clonal expansion, then antibody secretion.
options: Helper T activation, antibody secretion, antigen presentation, B cell expansion
Antigen presentation, helper T activation, B cell expansion, antibody secretion
B cell expansion, antigen presentation, antibody secretion, helper T activation
Antibody secretion, antigen presentation, helper T activation, B cell expansion
cards.explanation: An antigen presenting cell has to take up and display the antigen before any T cell can respond, the activated helper then licenses the matching B cell, the B cell clone expands, and only the plasma cells at the end of that chain secrete antibody. Every incorrect sequence here puts antibody or expansion before the recognition step that authorizes it, which is why a primary response takes several days rather than minutes.

cards.q: A patient clears extracellular bacteria normally but cannot control viruses inside cells and does not reject a skin graft. Which part of adaptive immunity is defective?
cards.a: The T cell arm, since both failures involve killing the body's own or foreign cells.
options: The complement system, since complement lyses infected body cells
The phagocytes, since phagocytes are what reject a transplanted graft
The T cell arm, since both failures involve killing whole cells
The B cell arm, since antibody is what clears virus inside cells
cards.explanation: Working backward from the findings: clearing extracellular bacteria proves antibody and phagocytes are working, and the two failures both require recognizing and destroying intact cells, which is exactly what cytotoxic T cells do. A B cell defect would show up as the opposite pattern, with extracellular infections predominating. Complement lyses bacteria rather than performing targeted killing of body cells, and phagocytes do not drive graft rejection.

cards.q: A vaccine produces good antibody but no cytotoxic T response against a virus that can spread directly from one cell to the next. Predict how well it protects.
cards.a: It blocks virus crossing between cells through the fluid but not virus passing cell to cell.
options: It blocks virus moving through the fluid but not virus passing cell to cell
It blocks both routes, since antibody reaches a virus wherever the virus goes
It blocks neither route, since antibody plays no part in antiviral defense
It blocks cell to cell spread but not free virus travelling in the blood
cards.explanation: Antibody patrols the extracellular space, so it intercepts free particles and can prevent the initial infection, but a virus that moves through direct contact between cells never enters that space and is never exposed. Clearing those infected cells requires the cytotoxic T response this vaccine failed to raise. The last option reverses the logic exactly, giving antibody access to the one route it cannot reach.

cards.q: How many polypeptide chains build one antibody monomer, and of which kinds?
cards.a: Four chains, two heavy and two light.
options: Four chains, two heavy and two light
Two chains, one heavy and one light
Six chains, four heavy and two light
Four chains, all four the same size
cards.explanation: Two long heavy chains pair with each other and each picks up a short light chain, giving the Y shaped monomer with four chains in total. Two chains would give only half a Y and only one binding site. Six chains and four identical chains do not match the symmetric two arm structure that lets a single antibody grip two identical epitopes at once.

cards.q: Which part of the antibody actually binds the antigen?
cards.a: The variable regions at the arm tips.
options: The hinge that sits between the two arms
The sugar groups attached to the stem
The variable regions at the tips of the arms
The constant region that makes up the stem
cards.explanation: The amino acid sequence at the arm tips differs from one antibody clone to the next, and that variability is what creates a pocket shaped for one epitope. The constant region of the stem is identical within a class and is read by phagocytes and complement rather than by antigen. The hinge sets how widely the arms can spread, and the attached sugars do not form the binding pocket.

cards.q: How many antigen binding sites does a single antibody monomer have?
cards.a: Two.
options: One
Two
Four
Ten
cards.explanation: Each arm of the Y carries one binding site, so a monomer such as IgG has two, and both sites bind the same epitope. Ten is the count for an IgM pentamer, which is five monomers joined together, so it is a real number for a real antibody but not for a monomer. One site would make bridging two targets impossible, which is why a monovalent fragment cannot agglutinate.

cards.q: What does the constant region of the heavy chain determine?
cards.a: The antibody class and which effector mechanisms the antibody can trigger.
options: How many antigen binding sites the monomer will carry
Whether the antibody folds correctly after it is made
The antibody class and the effector mechanisms it can trigger
Which particular antigen the antibody will be able to bind
cards.explanation: The stem is the handle: its sequence defines the class as IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, or IgD, and it decides whether complement can be fixed, whether a phagocyte receptor can bind it, and where the antibody is distributed. Antigen specificity comes from the variable tips instead. The number of binding sites depends on how many monomers join, not on the class alone, and folding is not what the constant region encodes.

cards.q: What is an epitope?
cards.a: The small region of an antigen that an antibody actually binds.
options: The small region of an antigen that an antibody actually binds
The binding pocket formed at the tip of the antibody arm
Any whole foreign protein that the body recognizes as nonself
The carbohydrate group that establishes the antibody class
cards.explanation: An antigen is usually a large molecule with several distinct surface patches, and each patch that a specific antibody can bind is an epitope, which is why one protein can raise several different antibodies. The pocket on the antibody side is the binding site, not the epitope, and swapping those two terms is the most common slip here. The whole molecule is the antigen rather than the epitope.

cards.q: Which antibody class appears first in a primary response and circulates as a pentamer?
cards.a: IgM.
options: IgE
IgM
IgG
IgA
cards.explanation: IgM is the first class a newly activated B cell secretes, and joining five monomers gives it ten binding sites, which makes it very effective at clumping antigen and at fixing complement even before affinity has improved. IgG appears later and dominates the secondary response. IgA is the secretory class of mucous surfaces and IgE is the class bound to mast cells.

cards.q: Which antibody class is most abundant in plasma and is the only one that crosses the placenta?
cards.a: IgG.
options: IgM
IgA
IgD
IgG
cards.explanation: IgG makes up roughly three quarters of plasma antibody, and its stem is recognized by a transport receptor in the placenta, so a fetus receives the mother's IgG before birth. IgM is too large a molecule to cross and stays in the bloodstream. IgA crosses into milk and other secretions rather than the placenta, and IgD sits on B cell surfaces with little role in plasma.

cards.q: Which antibody mechanism describes antibody binding a toxin so that the toxin cannot attach to a host cell?
cards.a: Neutralization.
options: Agglutination
Opsonization
Complement fixation
Neutralization
cards.explanation: Neutralization is pure blockade: the antibody covers the part of the toxin or virus that would have docked onto a cell, so the target is harmless even though nothing has been destroyed. Agglutination clumps particles together, opsonization tags a target for a phagocyte, and complement fixation recruits the cascade to lyse it. All four are antibody functions, so the distinction is what each one does to the target.

cards.q: Anti-A serum is mixed with a drop of a patient's blood on a slide and the red cells clump. Which mechanism produced the clumping, and what does the result tell you?
cards.a: Agglutination, so those red cells carry the A antigen.
options: Neutralization, so those red cells carry the A antigen
Agglutination, so those red cells lack the A antigen
Precipitation, so soluble A antigen is present in the plasma
Agglutination, so those red cells carry the A antigen
cards.explanation: Each antibody bridges two cells that both carry the epitope it binds, and thousands of such bridges form the visible clumps, so clumping with anti-A serum means the A antigen is on those cells. Neutralization blocks a toxin and produces nothing visible. Precipitation is the same bridging process acting on dissolved antigen rather than on cells, so it would not clump red cells.

cards.q: Why can a single antibody molecule link two separate bacterial cells together?
cards.a: Because it has two identical binding sites, one on each arm.
options: Because complement joins two antibody molecules end to end
Because it has two identical binding sites, one on each arm
Because its stem region binds a second bacterium directly
Because it changes shape to grip a new epitope after the first
cards.explanation: Both arms of a monomer carry the same specificity, so if two cells display the same epitope one antibody can hold one on each arm, and many antibodies doing this at once build a lattice. The stem binds phagocyte receptors and complement, not antigen. An antibody does not change its specificity after binding, and complement joining molecules together is not how a lattice forms.

cards.q: Antibody coats a bacterium. What does a neutrophil bind in order to engulf it more efficiently?
cards.a: The stem regions of the bound antibodies.
options: The bare bacterial surface between antibodies
The hinge segments where the arms bend
The stem regions of the bound antibodies
The variable tips that are holding the antigen
cards.explanation: Once the arms are occupied by antigen, the stems all point outward, and the phagocyte has receptors for exactly that region, so the coated bacterium is easy to grasp. That is opsonization by antibody, and it is why coating a slippery encapsulated organism makes such a difference. The variable tips are already engaged with the antigen, and the bare surface is what the phagocyte struggled with in the first place.

cards.q: Antibody binds a bacterial surface and complement is then activated at that spot. What happens to the bacterium?
cards.a: Complement assembles a pore in its membrane and it lyses.
options: Complement assembles a pore in its membrane, and it lyses
Complement digests the bacterial DNA and stops replication
Complement pulls the antibody off and recycles it for reuse
Complement blocks the bacterium from binding to host cells
cards.explanation: Antibody bound to a surface exposes a site on its stem that starts the classical complement pathway, and the cascade ends in a membrane attack complex that opens the cell to water and ions. Complement acts on the membrane, not on DNA. It does not remove the antibody, and blocking attachment to host cells is neutralization, which the antibody accomplishes on its own without complement.

cards.q: A mother's milk protects the lining of her infant's gut. Which antibody class does that, and where does it act?
cards.a: IgA, acting on the mucosal surface of the gut lumen.
options: IgM, acting on the lymph draining away from the intestine
IgA, acting on the mucosal surface facing the gut lumen
IgG, acting inside the infant's bloodstream after absorption
IgE, acting on mast cells within the wall of the intestine
cards.explanation: IgA is the class exported into secretions, including milk, saliva, and gut and airway mucus, and it works on the surface by blocking pathogens from ever attaching to the epithelium. IgG is the class transferred across the placenta into fetal blood, which is a different route for a different fluid. IgE arms mast cells for allergic responses, and IgM stays largely within the bloodstream.

cards.q: A patient's mast cells release histamine seconds after an antigen appears. Which antibody class was already bound to those mast cells?
cards.a: IgE.
options: IgM
IgA
IgE
IgG
cards.explanation: IgE is the one class whose stem binds mast cells and basophils, so it sits waiting on the cell surface long before the antigen arrives; when antigen links two of these antibodies together the cell degranulates immediately. IgG and IgM are free in plasma and produce slower responses involving complement and phagocytes. IgA is in secretions and does not arm mast cells.

cards.q: An enzyme cuts antibodies at the hinge, separating the two arms from the stem. Predict which antibody functions are kept and which are lost.
cards.a: Antigen binding is kept, while complement fixation and phagocyte binding are lost.
options: Antigen binding is kept, while complement fixation and phagocyte binding are lost
Antigen binding is lost, while complement fixation and phagocyte binding remain
Both antigen binding and every effector function are lost after the cut
Both antigen binding and every effector function survive the cut intact
cards.explanation: Function follows structure here: the binding pockets live in the arms and survive the cut, while the recognition surfaces that complement and phagocyte receptors read live in the stem and are separated away. The freed arms can still neutralize a toxin but can no longer recruit anything to destroy it. Losing binding while keeping effector function would require the opposite anatomy, with antigen recognized by the stem.

cards.q: A laboratory prepares antibody fragments that each carry only one binding site. Predict their effect on neutralizing a toxin and on agglutinating bacteria.
cards.a: They still neutralize the toxin but can no longer agglutinate bacteria.
options: They still agglutinate bacteria but can no longer neutralize the toxin
They perform both functions as well as the intact antibody does
They perform neither function, since one site cannot bind an epitope
They still neutralize the toxin but can no longer agglutinate bacteria
cards.explanation: Neutralization needs only occupancy: covering the active part of a toxin with one binding site is enough. Agglutination needs bridging, and bridging needs at least two sites on the same molecule so that two particles can be held together. A single site binds an epitope perfectly well, so the fragment is not useless, it has just lost every function that depended on holding two things at once.

cards.q: IgM has ten binding sites and IgG has two. Predict which clumps bacteria more efficiently per molecule, and why.
cards.a: IgM, because each molecule can bridge many more cells at once.
options: IgM, because its binding sites each hold antigen far more tightly
IgG, because clumping depends on the stem region rather than the arms
IgM, because each molecule can bridge many more cells at one time
IgG, because its smaller size lets it reach between cells more easily
cards.explanation: Clumping is a bridging problem, so the number of sites per molecule is what matters most, and a pentamer with ten sites builds a lattice with far fewer molecules than a monomer with two. IgM achieves this despite individual sites that bind less tightly than mature IgG sites, which is exactly why the site count and not the affinity is the deciding factor. The stem plays no part in holding antigen.

cards.q: A patient's antibodies bind their antigen normally but never activate complement. Working back from that result, which region is abnormal?
cards.a: The constant region of the heavy chain, which complement has to bind.
options: The hinge, which controls only how widely the two arms can spread
The constant region of the heavy chain, which complement has to bind
The variable region at the arm tips, which forms the binding pocket
The light chain, which by itself creates the antigen binding pocket
cards.explanation: Normal antigen binding proves the variable tips are intact, so the fault has to be downstream of binding, in the stem region that the first complement protein docks onto. A variable region defect would have shown up as failed binding instead. The light chain contributes to the pocket but does not form it alone, and a hinge defect would change flexibility and bridging rather than abolish complement activation outright.

cards.q: About how long after a first exposure does antibody become measurable in the plasma?
cards.a: About 3 to 6 days.
options: About 6 months
Within a few minutes
About 3 to 6 days
About 6 to 8 weeks
cards.explanation: The lag of the primary response is the time needed to find the one matching lymphocyte, activate it, expand the clone, and differentiate plasma cells, which takes several days and peaks around day 10 to 14. Minutes would describe an innate response or a preformed passive antibody. Weeks and months are far too long, which matters because it means a first infection is often over before antibody peaks.

cards.q: How quickly does a secondary response produce antibody after a repeat exposure?
cards.a: Within hours to two or three days.
options: After about two weeks of steady exposure
Only after a full month has passed
Within hours to two or three days
After the same 3 to 6 day lag as the first time
cards.explanation: Memory cells are already numerous and already specific, so the slow search and expansion phase of the primary response is skipped and antibody rises almost immediately. Repeating the original lag would mean no memory had formed at all. Longer delays describe no immune system a person could survive with, and the whole point of vaccination is buying this speed in advance.

cards.q: Which antibody class dominates the secondary response?
cards.a: IgG.
options: IgM
IgE
IgD
IgG
cards.explanation: Memory B cells have already switched their heavy chain constant region, so on a repeat exposure they secrete mostly IgG, which is longer lived in plasma and reaches the tissues more readily than IgM. IgM dominates the primary response and marks a recent first exposure, which is why the two classes are useful for dating an infection. IgE and IgD are minor in quantity and serve other roles.

cards.q: What is a memory B cell?
cards.a: A long lived descendant of an activated clone that waits in reserve for the same antigen.
options: A long lived descendant of an activated clone waiting for the same antigen
A plasma cell that keeps secreting antibody for the rest of a lifetime
A cell that stores antibody inside itself instead of releasing it
A cell that keeps a written record of every antigen the body has met
cards.explanation: When a clone expands, some daughters differentiate into antibody factories and others stay as small resting cells that persist for years, so the clone size for that one antigen is permanently larger. Plasma cells are short lived by comparison, which is why circulating antibody titer falls after an infection while protection persists. Memory cells do not stockpile antibody, they stand ready to make it.

cards.q: What defines active immunity?
cards.a: The person's own immune system responds and forms memory.
options: The person's own immune system responds and forms lasting memory
Ready made antibody is transferred in from another person or animal
Innate barriers block the pathogen before any lymphocyte is involved
A drug suppresses the pathogen while the immune system stays idle
cards.explanation: Active means the person did the work: antigen entered, lymphocytes were selected and expanded, and memory cells remain afterward. Transferred antibody is passive immunity, protective right away but leaving nothing behind. Innate barriers are not immunity in this sense at all, and a drug that clears an organism does not create any immunological memory.

cards.q: What defines passive immunity?
cards.a: Antibody made elsewhere is transferred in, giving immediate but temporary protection.
options: Phagocytes are stimulated to clear the pathogen without any antibody
Ready made antibody is transferred in, giving prompt short lived protection
The person makes antibody after a weakened form of the pathogen is given
Memory cells are transferred so the recipient responds faster next time
cards.explanation: In passive immunity the recipient contributes nothing but a bloodstream: the antibody works from the moment it arrives and then degrades over weeks, leaving no memory cells and no lasting protection. Making antibody after a weakened pathogen is artificial active immunity, the definition of vaccination. Clinical passive transfer moves antibody rather than cells, and phagocyte stimulation is not what the term describes.

cards.q: A newborn is protected for several months by antibody received across the placenta. Which type of immunity is that?
cards.a: Natural passive immunity.
options: Natural active immunity
Artificial passive immunity
Artificial active immunity
Natural passive immunity
cards.explanation: It is passive because the antibody came from the mother rather than from the infant's own response, and natural because it happened without any medical intervention. Natural active would mean the infant caught an infection and responded. Artificial passive covers the same transfer done deliberately, as with an injection of immune globulin, and artificial active is vaccination.

cards.q: A person receives a vaccine containing an inactivated virus. Which type of immunity does this produce?
cards.a: Artificial active immunity.
options: Natural passive immunity
Artificial active immunity
Artificial passive immunity
Natural active immunity
cards.explanation: Active because the recipient's own lymphocytes recognize the antigen and build memory, and artificial because the exposure was deliberately arranged rather than an infection. Artificial passive would mean receiving antibody rather than antigen. Natural active immunity comes from actually catching the disease, which produces the same kind of memory at a much higher cost.

cards.q: A patient bitten by a venomous snake is given antivenom containing antibodies against the venom. Predict when protection begins and whether memory forms.
cards.a: Protection is immediate and no memory forms.
options: Protection is immediate and no memory forms afterward
Protection begins in about a week and lasting memory forms
Protection is immediate and lasting memory forms afterward
Protection begins in about a week and no memory forms
cards.explanation: Transferred antibody is already made, so it starts neutralizing venom as soon as it circulates, which is the entire reason passive transfer is used in an emergency. Nothing in the patient's own lymphocyte population has been selected or expanded, so once the transferred protein degrades over the following weeks, protection ends. A second bite later would find the patient no better prepared than the first.

cards.q: A child recovers from chickenpox and is protected for decades afterward. Which type of immunity did the illness produce?
cards.a: Natural active immunity.
options: Natural passive immunity
Artificial active immunity
Artificial passive immunity
Natural active immunity
cards.explanation: The child's own lymphocytes met the virus, expanded, and left memory cells behind, so the immunity is active, and because the exposure came from ordinary infection rather than a clinic, it is natural. Passive labels would require antibody arriving from someone else, which would not last decades. Artificial active would mean the same memory produced by a vaccine instead of by the disease.

cards.q: Why does a booster dose of a vaccine raise antibody higher than the first dose did?
cards.a: The first dose left a larger population of memory cells specific for that antigen.
options: The second dose is given by a route that the body absorbs more quickly
The first dose left a much larger population of memory cells for that antigen
The second dose always contains a larger quantity of the antigen
The first dose left circulating antibody that adds to the second response
cards.explanation: Response size scales with how many matching lymphocytes are available at the moment of exposure, and the first dose converted a handful of cells into a large standing memory clone. Booster doses are not larger in antigen content, and the leftover antibody from the first dose is usually low and does not explain a ten fold or greater rise. Route of administration does not change the size of the clone that responds.

cards.q: Maternal antibody in an infant falls to very low levels by about six months of age. What does this predict about the infant's susceptibility?
cards.a: Susceptibility rises, because the borrowed protection fades and none of it was replaced by memory.
options: Susceptibility rises, because borrowed protection fades and left no memory
Susceptibility falls, because the infant has now formed its own memory cells
Susceptibility stays unchanged, because memory cells came across with the antibody
Susceptibility rises briefly and then falls again without any further exposure
cards.explanation: Placental transfer moves antibody protein, not cells, so when that protein degrades the infant has nothing left over from it, and this window is exactly why the childhood vaccination schedule begins when it does. Forming memory would require the infant's own response to an antigen. Protection cannot return on its own without exposure to the antigen or another vaccine.

cards.q: A patient receives immune globulin against hepatitis A after an exposure. If they are exposed again two years later, what will their response be?
cards.a: A primary response, because the transferred antibody left no memory.
options: No response at all, because the earlier globulin suppressed their immunity
An immediate response, because some of the transferred antibody still remains
A primary response, because the transferred antibody left no memory behind
A secondary response, because the transferred antibody trained their B cells
cards.explanation: Passive antibody protects while it is present and teaches nothing, so two years later the patient meets that virus as if for the first time, with the full several day lag. Transferred antibody does not instruct B cells. It also does not permanently suppress immunity, and injected immunoglobulin is gone within a few months, far short of two years.

cards.q: A first vaccine dose raises antibody titer to 100 units and a booster raises it to 1600 units. What does that sixteen fold difference reflect?
cards.a: A far larger population of antigen specific cells responding this time.
options: A change in the antigen itself between the first and second injections
A far larger population of antigen specific cells responding this time
A stronger innate response to the second injection at the same site
A slower breakdown of antibody protein after the second dose is given
cards.explanation: The magnitude of an antibody response tracks the number of responding cells, and clonal expansion during the first dose left thousands of memory cells where there had been very few. Innate responses do not produce antigen specific antibody. Antibody breakdown rates do not change with dose number, and the antigen in a booster is deliberately the same as in the first dose.

cards.q: Why does a vaccine given today not protect a traveler who leaves tomorrow?
cards.a: Active immunity requires days to weeks for clonal expansion and antibody production.
options: Vaccines only work if they are given after exposure rather than before
The antigen in a vaccine has to be swallowed to reach the immune system
Antibody made from a vaccine is destroyed during the first day after injection
Active immunity needs days to weeks for clonal expansion and antibody output
cards.explanation: A vaccine supplies antigen, not protection, and the recipient still has to run the primary response, which takes about two weeks to reach useful titer. If protection is needed immediately, the only option is passive transfer of preformed antibody. Vaccines are given before exposure precisely because of this lag, and injected antigen reaches lymph nodes without needing to be swallowed.

cards.q: After a high risk animal bite a patient is given both immune globulin against rabies and the rabies vaccine. Explain what each contributes to protection over time.
cards.a: The globulin protects immediately while the vaccine builds lasting protection over the following weeks.
options: The globulin protects immediately while the vaccine builds protection over weeks
The vaccine protects immediately while the globulin builds protection over weeks
Both protect immediately, so giving the two together is simply a precaution
Both take weeks to work, so protection cannot begin until the second week
cards.explanation: The two are given together because they cover different parts of the same timeline: preformed antibody neutralizes virus from the moment it is injected but fades, while the vaccine antigen starts a primary response that takes about two weeks and then persists as memory. Reversing them misreads which one is antibody and which is antigen. If both worked immediately, or neither did, there would be no reason to give two products at once.

cards.q: Antibody appears on day 5 after a first exposure, peaks on day 12, is mostly IgM, and falls by day 30. A second exposure on day 60 gives antibody by day 2, ten times higher, mostly IgG. What accounts for the differences?
cards.a: Memory cells from the first exposure that are numerous and already class switched.
options: A larger dose of antigen on the second exposure than on the first exposure
Memory cells from the first exposure, numerous and already class switched
Antibody left over from the first exposure that was reactivated by the antigen
A stronger innate response on the second exposure that produced the IgG
cards.explanation: Three features change together, and one mechanism explains all three: memory cells are present in large numbers so the lag shortens and the peak rises, and they have already switched their heavy chain so the output is IgG rather than IgM. Leftover antibody had already fallen by day 30 and antibody molecules cannot be reactivated. Innate responses never make antibody, and nothing in the description says the dose changed.

cards.q: A patient who cannot make B cells receives an infusion of pooled immune globulin every four weeks. Predict their protection between infusions and whether they will ever need to stop.
cards.a: They are protected while the antibody lasts, form no memory, and need the infusions indefinitely.
options: Unprotected between doses, because transferred antibody acts only on the day given
Protected permanently after several doses, because the antibody stimulates B cells
Protected while the antibody lasts, no memory forms, and infusions go on
Protected while the antibody lasts, and memory builds so the infusions can stop
cards.explanation: Passive antibody is a supply, not a lesson: it works from the moment it is given, degrades over a few weeks, and leaves no cells behind, so the schedule is set by the half life of the protein rather than by any developing response. A patient with no B cells cannot make memory, so the treatment cannot become self sustaining. The antibody does last between doses, which is exactly why a four week interval works.

cards.q: A person exposed to the same virus twice became ill the first time but not the second, although their antibody titer was near zero just before the second exposure. Explain the protection.
cards.a: Memory cells responded within a day or two, before the virus could establish an infection.
options: Standing antibody must have been present but was too low for the test to detect
Innate defenses were permanently strengthened by the first infection
The virus had weakened between the first and the second exposure
Memory cells responded within a day or two, before the virus could establish itself
cards.explanation: Protection does not require antibody circulating at all times; it requires the ability to produce antibody faster than the pathogen can gain ground, and a memory clone does that within a couple of days. This is why a low titer years after vaccination does not necessarily mean protection has been lost. Innate defenses do not strengthen with experience, and nothing here suggests the virus itself changed.

cards.q: What is the immune system doing wrong in an allergy?
cards.a: It is mounting a strong response against a harmless foreign substance.
options: It is mounting a strong response against a harmless foreign substance
It is attacking the body's own tissues as though they were foreign
It is failing to respond because a needed component is missing
It is responding normally but far too slowly to be of any use
cards.explanation: In allergy the machinery works, the specificity works, and the target is genuinely foreign; the error is that the antigen posed no threat, so the damage comes from the response rather than from the pollen or the peanut. Attacking self tissue is autoimmunity and failing for lack of a component is immunodeficiency. Sorting these three by what has gone wrong is the whole of this competency.

cards.q: What is the immune system doing wrong in an autoimmune disease?
cards.a: It has lost tolerance and is attacking the body's own tissues.
options: It is overreacting to a harmless substance from outside the body
It cannot produce enough lymphocytes to fight ordinary infections
It responds only to antigens it has already encountered once before
It has lost tolerance and is attacking the body's own tissues
