cards.explanation: Self tolerance is normally established by removing or silencing lymphocytes whose receptors match self molecules, and autoimmunity is the failure of that screening, so a normal immune attack is aimed at the wrong tissue. Overreacting to an outside antigen is allergy, in which the target really is foreign. A shortage of lymphocytes describes immunodeficiency, and responding to previously seen antigens is normal memory.

cards.q: What is the immune system doing wrong in an immunodeficiency?
cards.a: A component is missing or not working, so responses are too weak.
options: A response is aimed at a self antigen instead of a foreign one
A response is far larger than the threat from the antigen warrants
A response is aimed at the correct antigen but in the wrong tissue
A component is missing or not working, so responses are too weak
cards.explanation: Immunodeficiency is a failure of capacity: a missing cell type, antibody class, or complement protein leaves a gap, and the patient presents with infections that a normal immune system would clear. Misdirected responses against self are autoimmunity and oversized responses to harmless antigens are allergy, so the three categories differ by whether the problem is too little, misaimed, or too much.

cards.q: Which combination triggers the immediate symptoms of an allergic reaction?
cards.a: IgE bound to mast cells, which release histamine when antigen binds.
options: IgM bound to red cells, which release histamine when complement binds
IgA bound to plasma cells, which release cytokines when antigen binds
IgE bound to mast cells, which release histamine when antigen binds
IgG bound to neutrophils, which release lysozyme when antigen binds
cards.explanation: Sensitization puts IgE on mast cell surfaces during the first exposure, and on a later exposure the antigen bridges two of those antibodies and the cell degranulates within seconds, releasing histamine and producing the familiar symptoms. Neutrophils and red cells do not carry the granules or the receptors involved. Plasma cells secrete antibody and do not display it on their surface for this purpose.

cards.q: What happens to blood vessels and airways during anaphylaxis?
cards.a: Vessels dilate and leak while airway smooth muscle constricts.
options: Vessels dilate and airway smooth muscle relaxes at the same time
Vessels constrict and leak while airway smooth muscle constricts
Vessels dilate and leak while airway smooth muscle constricts
Vessels constrict while airway smooth muscle relaxes and opens
cards.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a local allergic response occurring body wide, so the histamine effects you would see in one swollen finger happen everywhere at once: widespread vasodilation and leak drop blood pressure while bronchoconstriction closes the airway. Vasoconstriction and bronchodilation are the opposite pattern and are what treatment aims to restore. The danger comes from both systems failing at once.

cards.q: Which cell does HIV infect and destroy?
cards.a: The helper T cell.
options: The red blood cell
The helper T cell
The plasma cell
The neutrophil
cards.explanation: HIV enters cells carrying the CD4 surface protein, and the helper T cell is the main one, which is why a virus that infects a single cell type dismantles so much of the immune system. Plasma cells and neutrophils are not the virus target, though both function poorly once helper T support is gone. Red cells have no nucleus and cannot support viral replication.

cards.q: A patient sneezes and develops watery eyes every spring when tree pollen is in the air. Classify this and name the error.
cards.a: Allergy, since a strong response is aimed at a harmless foreign antigen.
options: Immunodeficiency, since the response fails to clear the pollen entirely
A normal response, since pollen is foreign and should be attacked hard
Allergy, since a strong response is aimed at a harmless foreign antigen
Autoimmunity, since the response is aimed at the patient's own tissue
cards.explanation: Pollen is foreign but harmless, and the symptoms come entirely from the patient's own histamine release rather than from anything the pollen does, which is the definition of an allergic response. The target is not self, so this is not autoimmunity. It is not immunodeficiency either, since the response is vigorous rather than weak, and calling it normal ignores the fact that most people inhale pollen with no symptoms at all.

cards.q: A patient's blood contains antibodies that bind and damage their own thyroid cells. Classify this and name the error.
cards.a: Autoimmunity, since self tolerance for a thyroid antigen has failed.
options: Autoimmunity, since self tolerance for a thyroid antigen has failed
Allergy, since the antibody was raised against an outside substance
Immunodeficiency, since the thyroid can no longer defend itself
A normal response, since damaged cells are always targeted this way
cards.explanation: The antibody is specific, well made, and working exactly as designed; the failure is in tolerance, because a B cell clone that should have been eliminated for recognizing a self antigen was allowed to mature. Allergy would require the antigen to come from outside the body. The immune system here is too active rather than deficient, and healthy self tissue is not normally attacked by antibody.

cards.q: A young child has repeated bacterial infections and blood tests show almost no antibody of any class. Classify this and name the error.
cards.a: Immunodeficiency, since a needed component of the response is absent.
options: Autoimmunity, since antibody is being destroyed by the patient's own cells
Allergy, since the repeated infections have sensitized the child's mast cells
A normal finding, since young children do not produce antibody at all
Immunodeficiency, since a needed component of the response is absent
cards.explanation: Recurrent infection plus a missing component is the signature of immunodeficiency, and the absent antibody points to the B cell arm specifically, which fits the bacterial pattern of infection. Nothing here describes an attack on self tissue or a response to a harmless antigen. Children do produce their own antibody, beginning in the first months of life as maternal antibody fades, so this is not a normal age related finding.

cards.q: Predict what happens to arterial blood pressure during anaphylaxis, and why.
cards.a: It falls, because widespread vasodilation and fluid leak reduce both resistance and blood volume.
options: It falls, because dilation and fluid leak cut both resistance and volume
It rises, because the immune response raises cardiac output sharply
It stays steady, because histamine acts on airways rather than vessels
It falls, because histamine directly stops the heart from contracting
cards.explanation: Two histamine effects push pressure the same direction at once: dilating arterioles everywhere lowers total peripheral resistance, and increased capillary permeability moves plasma into the tissues so venous return falls too. Since pressure depends on both, the drop can be severe. Histamine acts strongly on vessels as well as airways, and the fall is a vascular problem rather than a failure of cardiac contraction.

cards.q: Epinephrine reverses the dangerous changes of anaphylaxis. Which two actions does it provide?
cards.a: Vasoconstriction to raise blood pressure and bronchodilation to open the airway.
options: Vasodilation to improve perfusion and bronchoconstriction to trap more oxygen
Vasoconstriction to raise blood pressure and bronchodilation to open the airway
Vasodilation to improve tissue perfusion and bronchodilation to open the airway
Vasoconstriction to raise blood pressure and bronchoconstriction to slow airflow
cards.explanation: Epinephrine acts on alpha receptors in vascular smooth muscle to constrict vessels and on beta receptors in airway smooth muscle to relax them, which is precisely the opposite of what histamine did to each tissue. Adding more vasodilation would deepen the fall in pressure. Bronchoconstriction would worsen the airway obstruction, and trapping air is not a benefit in any respiratory situation.

cards.q: Three patients: the first makes antibody against their own joint tissue, the second collapses minutes after eating peanut, the third has fungal infections that never fully clear. Classify them in order.
cards.a: Autoimmunity, allergy, immunodeficiency.
options: Autoimmunity, immunodeficiency, allergy
Autoimmunity, allergy, immunodeficiency
Allergy, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency
Immunodeficiency, allergy, autoimmunity
cards.explanation: Sort by what is wrong rather than by how sick the patient looks. Antibody against self tissue is a tolerance failure, a violent response within minutes of a harmless food is an IgE driven allergy, and infections that a normal immune system would clear point to a missing or failing component. Persistent fungal infection in particular suggests a T cell problem, since cell mediated immunity handles those organisms.

cards.q: As HIV destroys helper T cells over years, predict what happens to cell mediated immunity and to antibody responses, and what the patient develops as a result.
cards.a: Both arms weaken and infections appear that a healthy immune system would clear.
options: Only cell mediated immunity weakens, so antibody responses stay fully normal
Only antibody responses weaken, so cell mediated immunity stays fully normal
Both arms strengthen at first, so the patient resists infection unusually well
Both arms weaken and infections appear that a healthy system would clear
cards.explanation: The helper T cell sits upstream of both arms, licensing cytotoxic T cells and providing the cytokines most B cells need, so destroying it produces a combined deficiency even though only one cell type is infected. That is why the illnesses that follow include organisms handled by antibody and organisms handled by cell mediated immunity. Expecting only one arm to fail underestimates how central the helper T cell is.

cards.q: A patient has normal antibody levels, normal T cell counts, and no unusual infections, but has painful inflamed joints and antibodies in the blood that bind their own cartilage. Working from these findings, classify the disorder.
cards.a: Autoimmunity, since the response is intact and specific but directed at self.
options: Allergy, since the joint inflammation follows exposure to an outside antigen
Two disorders at once, since inflammation and antibody cannot share one cause
Autoimmunity, since the response is intact and specific but directed at self
Immunodeficiency, since inflamed joints show the defenses cannot cope
cards.explanation: Normal counts and no unusual infections rule out immunodeficiency, and nothing foreign is described, which rules out allergy, leaving self directed antibody as the finding that explains the joint damage. The inflammation is the expected consequence of that antibody binding tissue and recruiting the inflammatory response, so one mechanism accounts for both findings rather than two separate disorders.
